Plots of a fitted model

Source: vignettes/plots.Rmd
plots.Rmd

This vignette shows what each plot function in bayesEfron is for and how to read the result. A fit contains a posterior distribution for \(g\), the distribution of effects, and for the effect of every site, and most questions about it are easier to answer from a plot than from a table.

library(bayesEfron)

Each plot function returns a ggplot object that you can change with ggplot2 functions. The one exception is plot_mcmc(type = "pairs"), which returns the grid of plots that bayesplot makes.

For most examples we use two fits stored in the package: krw_fit, the callback gaps of 97 firms from vignette("bayesEfron"), and twin_towers_fit, 1,500 simulated sites with known true effects from vignette("twin-towers").

firms <- krw_fit
sims <- twin_towers_fit
truth <- twin_towers$theta_true

The distribution of effects

plot_g() shows what the distribution of true effects looks like and how well the data determine it. The curve is the posterior mean of the density of \(g\), and the pointwise band around it contains the density with the stated probability at each value. Below, observed puts a histogram of the estimates under the curve, normal puts a normal distribution fitted to the same estimates over it, and scale = 100 gives percentage points.

plot_g(firms, observed = "histogram", normal = TRUE, scale = 100)

The histogram is wider than the curve because the estimates contain sampling error and the effects do not. Where the band is wide, the data do not determine the height of the density well.

Proportions of sites are easier to read from the distribution function, so next we set type = "cdf". Setting inner_level adds a second, narrower band.

plot_g(firms, type = "cdf", inner_level = 0.5, scale = 100)

The height of the curve at a value is the proportion of firms with a gap below it. Three more arguments add to the plot:

  • draws = 40 adds 40 posterior draws of \(g\) to its posterior mean and band.
  • truth adds the true effects of simulated data.
  • compare puts other estimates of the distribution over this one, from other fits or from other software.

The sites

Caterpillar plot

A caterpillar plot from plot_sites() shows the posterior mean of each site with a 50% and a 90% interval, and the estimate as an open circle. Use it to see which sites have the largest and the smallest effects, and how certain that ordering is.

plot_sites(firms, n_extreme = 10, scale = 100)

n_extreme selects the sites at the two ends, and sites selects sites by name or position. Without either, every site is plotted: labeled when there are at most 100, and as thin lines when there are more.

plot_sites(sims)

Shrinkage plot

plot_shrinkage() shows how far the model moves the estimates by plotting the posterior mean of every site against its estimate. Points on the diagonal have not moved.

plot_shrinkage(firms, scale = 100)

With style = "arrows", each site is an arrow from the estimate to the posterior mean, at the height of its standard error. This suits a small number of sites, such as the 19 teacher expectancy studies in the stored fit raudenbush_fit.

plot_shrinkage(raudenbush_fit, style = "arrows")

Exceedance probabilities

When the question is which sites have an effect above a threshold, plot_exceedance() plots, for each site, the posterior probability that its effect is above the threshold. cutoff marks a probability and counts the sites that reach it. For many sites, the probabilities are plotted as a curve.

plot_exceedance(sims, cutoff = 0.9)

The caption notes that the count controls no error rate over the sites, which is easy to forget when a list of sites is made from it.

The posterior of one site

plot_site_posterior() plots the whole posterior distribution of a site, with the two things that it is made from: the likelihood of the estimate and the estimate of \(g\).

plot_site_posterior(sims, sites = c(268, 304))

The first site has an imprecise estimate between the two groups of simulated effects, and its posterior distribution has two modes. A mean and an interval would hide that.

Checking a fit

Sampler and grid diagnostics

plot_diagnostics() plots what diagnose() reports, so you can check two things at once: whether the sampler converged, and whether the grid suits the fit. R-hat and the effective sample sizes of the quantities that the sampler records are shown in blocks against their thresholds, with two more panels about the grid.

plot_diagnostics(firms)

Points to the right of the dashed line in the first panel (R-hat), or to the left of it in the next two (effective sample sizes), would be quantities that miss their thresholds. There are none here. The caption gives the numbers of divergent transitions and of iterations at the maximum tree depth, and vignette("diagnostics") explains each check.

Posterior predictive check

A posterior predictive check with plot_ppc() shows whether the model reproduces the estimates. The check compares each estimate with the distribution that the fitted model gives it, through the probability of a smaller estimate at that site (the probability integral transform, PIT). If \(g\) were known, these values would be uniformly distributed between 0 and 1, and the line shows how far the values of the fitted model are from that.

plot_ppc(firms)

The band is the reference for independent uniform values, but it does not allow for the fitting of \(g\). See vignette("diagnostics") for how to read it.

Pareto k values

Leave-one-out cross-validation approximates the fit that would result without each site, and the Pareto k of a site measures how good that approximation is. To check that the approximation is reliable for every site, plot the values with plot_loo(). A line marks the value above which the result for a site should not be trusted, and the sites above it are labeled. See vignette("diagnostics") for more.

plot_loo(firms)

Grids and grid comparisons

The plot() method for a grid, or plot(fit, type = "grid") for the grid of a fit, shows where the grid lies in relation to the data: the spline functions, the knots and the grid points over the estimates.

plot(sims, type = "grid")

The limits of this grid are well inside the range of the estimates because the default grid_method narrowed it.

To see what changes when the grid changes, plot a comparison from compare_efron_grids(): the specifications appear one under the other. Here we load a stored comparison of three ranges for the 19 teacher expectancy studies.

comparison <- readRDS(system.file("examples", "raudenbush_ranges.rds",
                                  package = "bayesEfron"))
plot(comparison)

vignette("twin-towers") discusses the first of these plots and vignette("teacher-expectancy") the second.

Simulated data

With simulated data, plot_recovery() shows how close a fit comes to the known effects. It plots the intervals of the sites with the true effects and marks the sites where the true effect is outside. Only 150 sites are shown, and seed fixes the random choice.

plot_recovery(sims, truth, seed = 1)

Setting type = "calibration" shows the proportion of true effects inside the intervals at every level from 5% to 95%, and type = "scatter" plots the posterior means against the true effects.

Common arguments

Every plot function takes the fit first, and a few arguments work the same way wherever they apply:

  • scale multiplies the effect values. For example, scale = 100 turns differences in probabilities into percentage points.
  • level sets the probability of posterior intervals and bands. In plot_ppc() it sets the level of the independent-uniform reference intervals.
  • sites and highlight take positions or labels.

Calling plot() on a fit with a type runs the same functions by name, so plot(firms, type = "g", scale = 100) is the same as plot_g(firms, scale = 100).

Customizing a plot

A plot has no title, but its caption says what the lines and bands are. You can set both, and add layers, as with any other ggplot object:

plot_g(firms, scale = 100) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted") +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Callback gaps of 97 firms",
                x = "White minus Black callback rate (percentage points)")

Making your own plots

The numbers in the plots of \(g\) and of the sites are also available from three functions. The densities, distribution functions and probabilities of \(g\) come from g_summary(), the means and intervals of the sites from site_summary(), and the probabilities of exceeding a threshold from exceedance_prob(). To make a plot that the package does not have, start from these functions:

head(g_summary(firms, type = "cdf", scale = 100), 3)
#>       value         mean        lower        upper
#> 1 -8.289621 0.0002198804 2.447210e-07 0.0008876288
#> 2 -8.048199 0.0005935610 7.766047e-07 0.0024197491
#> 3 -7.806777 0.0008606321 1.298678e-06 0.0034986411
site_summary(firms, sites = c("KFC", "Walmart"), scale = 100)[, 1:8]
#>   site   label estimate       se     mean       sd      lower    upper
#> 1    2     KFC      2.2 1.530472 1.786494 1.052594 0.12271869 3.581179
#> 2   65 Walmart      7.0 3.919826 2.386823 1.744476 0.04493205 5.523267

MCMC plots with bayesplot

Trace plots, rank plots and the other plots of the Markov chains come from bayesplot, and plot_mcmc() passes the draws of a fit to it. We show a rank plot, in which the draws of all the chains are ranked together and each line counts the ranks of one chain in 20 bins. Chains that sample the same distribution give lines that overlap around a common level, as they do here.

plot_mcmc(firms, type = "rank", pars = c("lambda", "sd_g"))

The type argument can be "trace", "rank", "dens", "pairs" or "energy", and vignette("diagnostics") shows a trace plot. For anything else, pass the draws and the sampler’s quantities to bayesplot yourself:

bayesplot::mcmc_areas(firms$draws, pars = c("mean_g", "sd_g"))
bayesplot::mcmc_nuts_divergence(bayesplot::nuts_params(firms),
                                bayesplot::log_posterior(firms))

Note that the stored fits are thinned to 1 draw in 15, so their trace plots show 200 draws for each chain, whereas the sampler diagnostics in plot_diagnostics() are computed from the whole run. The energy plot compares each iteration with the one before it and is available only for a fit that stores every iteration. See vignette("diagnostics") for the call.
